case_study_insert.main_stem: Kestrel Medical Supplies (KMS) is a private limited company in the healthcare sector, employing a workforce of 50. Founded in 2011 by Priya Kestrel, it manufactures sterile wound-care dressings for hospital groups and operates a hierarchical structure with democratic leadership. KMS plans to invest $720,000 in an automated sterile-dressing line, financed by a $420,000 ten-year bank loan and $300,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $240,000 a year, a variable cost of $5.50 a unit and a selling price of $10.50, and currently produces 110,000 units a year. Its main hospital contracts require delivery within 48 hours, and it prides itself on a strong sterility record. KMS faces two problems: absenteeism has reached 8% and complaints about torn sterile packaging are rising.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Quality and Operations Report, Q4 2025: The sterile dressing line packed 27,500 units last quarter at a defect rate of 2.4%, down from 4.0% a year earlier. Customer complaints about torn packaging fell from 44 to 19 per month. Average order fulfilment is 4.1 days. A survey of 500 hospital procurement staff found 68% would pay up to $0.30 more for tamper-evident packs and 57% check sterility certification before ordering. Records show 18 of 50 staff have not completed on-the-job training on the new sealing machines; external certification courses cost $780 per employee.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Profit or Loss and Capital employed data of Kestrel Medical Supplies for the year ended 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 4.25% to 5.0%, increasing borrowing costs for firms with variable-rate loans. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 5.8% from $13.00 to $13.75 per hour, raising wage bills across healthcare manufacturing. (3) Wholesale non-woven fabric and packaging input costs have risen 9.6% year-on-year, medical-consumables inflation is 6.2%, and hospital procurement spending grew 2.8% over the same period.

questions.question_text: KMS plans to fund part of its $720,000 sterile-dressing line with a $420,000 ten-year bank loan. Explain two advantages for KMS of using retained profit rather than the bank loan.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Retained profit carries no interest charges or compulsory repayments, so the $300,000 KMS sets aside from past profits protects its cash flow while it services fixed costs of $240,000 a year. Every dollar not paid as interest can absorb the 9.6% rise in fabric and packaging input costs without pushing the $10.50 selling price above what hospital groups will accept, preserving the $5.00 contribution per unit on 110,000 units.

Point 2: Using retained profit avoids the security and default risk of the $420,000 loan, so the new automated line cannot be repossessed if hospital orders fall short. It also leaves Priya Kestrel's ownership and control intact, since no lender can attach conditions to how the sterile-dressing line is run. Retained profit is immediately available with no application delay, letting KMS respond quickly to the torn-packaging complaints and begin the 48-hour delivery improvements its hospital contracts demand. Together these advantages let KMS direct scarce cash toward the 8% absenteeism problem and the torn-packaging complaints rather than toward a lender.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage of retained profit over a bank loan (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation applied to KMS, its $720,000 line, costs and hospital contracts.

questions.question_text: KMS is launching new tamper-evident sterile packs. Consider advertising in national hospital-supply journals, sponsoring a large hospital conference, or targeted email and social media marketing to procurement staff. Which should KMS choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
National trade-journal advertising: A campaign in hospital-supply journals would reach procurement departments across the country and lend KMS credibility as a sterile-dressing supplier. Print production and placement costs are high, however, and much of the readership will not be in a position to switch supplier, so the spend is largely wasted for a 50-employee firm committing $720,000 to a new line. Results are also slow to arrive and hard to measure.

Hospital conference sponsorship: Sponsoring a major clinical conference puts KMS in front of the exact sterile-pack decision-makers and allows live demonstration of the tamper-evident seal, which directly answers the 68% of surveyed procurement staff who would pay $0.30 more and the 57% who check sterility certification. The drawbacks are a very high one-off cost and a single event with limited reach; with 500 staff surveyed and only 27,500 units packed last quarter, one conference cannot on its own sustain the 110,000-unit output target.

Targeted email and social media marketing: Direct digital marketing to procurement staff lets KMS show the tamper-evident design and certification to precisely the segment its research identified, at low cost per contact and with measurable responses. Messages can be updated quickly to reflect the falling 2.4% defect rate. Its weakness is that procurement decisions are relationship-driven and digital messages can be ignored, so it works best alongside personal follow-up.

Recommendation: KMS should choose targeted email and social media marketing, supported by a small conference presence. It reaches the 68% willing to pay $0.30 more and the 57% checking certification far more cheaply than national print, and unlike a single conference it can run continuously to support 110,000 units of output. National journals are rejected as expensive and untargeted; full conference sponsorship is rejected as too costly and one-off for a business already funding a $420,000 loan.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies promotional options with limited reference to KMS's survey or product.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Discusses advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of KMS with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Evaluates all three options in context with a justified recommendation that explains why national journals and conference sponsorship are rejected.

questions.question_text: KMS has a hierarchical structure with democratic leadership and has seen absenteeism reach 8%. Explain two benefits for KMS of introducing quality circles to reduce its 2.4% defect rate and absenteeism.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Quality circles give the 50 production staff a regular forum to identify the causes of torn sterile packaging, such as sealing-machine settings or handling steps. Because the operators themselves diagnose problems, solutions are practical and quickly applied, which should push the current 2.4% defect rate below the 4.0% recorded a year ago and cut rework on the 27,500 units packed last quarter.

Point 2: Involving staff in quality decisions raises ownership and job satisfaction, directly addressing the 8% absenteeism rate. Workers who help set packing routines are more likely to attend and to follow sterility procedures, protecting the 48-hour delivery promise in hospital contracts. Democratic leadership already encourages consultation, so quality circles fit KMS's culture and cost little compared with the $780 external certification course, while easing pressure on the $720,000 automated line. The same forum can review the 19 complaints a month still received, turning customer feedback into practical packing improvements while the $420,000 loan is serviced.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit of quality circles (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual development linked to KMS's defect rate, absenteeism, workforce and delivery commitments.

questions.question_text: KMS must train 18 of its 50 staff on the new sealing machines. Consider on-the-job training or external certification courses costing $780 per employee. Which should KMS choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
On-the-job training: Training at the sterile-dressing line is specific to KMS's own sealing machines and quality standards, costs no course fees and keeps the 18 staff productive while they learn. That protects the 27,500 units packed last quarter and the improvement from a 4.0% to a 2.4% defect rate. Weaknesses are that trainer-operators lose some output themselves, bad habits can spread, and there is no external certificate, which may matter when hospital auditors check the sterility certification that 57% of buyers look for. Some formal proof will therefore be needed eventually, but it need not be purchased for all 18 staff at once, and on-the-job coaching keeps the $720,000 line running at full capacity.

External certification courses: At $780 per employee, certificating all 18 staff costs $14,040 ($780 x 18) — small beside the $720,000 investment. The course gives structured, up-to-date skills and a recognised qualification that supports those certification-conscious buyers. However, it removes 18 of 50 workers from the line temporarily, cutting capacity at a time when absenteeism is already 8%, and generic content may not match KMS's exact machine settings, so follow-up coaching would still be needed.

Decision: KMS should choose on-the-job training for the initial rollout, with short external certification later for senior operators. It is cheapest, machine-specific and avoids losing output while absenteeism is 8%; full external training is rejected because withdrawing $14,040 and 18 staff from the line would disrupt the 48-hour delivery commitment and the 110,000-unit plan, and KMS can add certificates once the line is stable.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Describes the two training methods with little application to KMS.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the benefits and drawbacks of each method in the context of KMS's costs, output and staffing.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both methods with a justified decision that rejects the alternative and refers to cost, disruption and machine relevance.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how KMS's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $240,000 ÷ ($10.50 − $5.50) = $240,000 ÷ $5.00 = 48,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 48,000 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $10.50 − $5.50 = $5.00. Answer: contribution per unit is $5.00.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways KMS's management can use this cost and break-even data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. Compare the 48,000-unit break-even output with actual output of 110,000 units to find a margin of safety of 62,000 units (110,000 − 48,000), showing the $720,000 line can absorb a demand shortfall.
2. Use the $5.00 contribution to test the survey finding: at 110,000 units an extra $0.30 would add $33,000 of contribution (110,000 x $0.30), helping fund the $780 certification courses.
3. Check that contribution covers fixed costs of $240,000 and interest on the $420,000 loan before adding capacity, so financing costs do not push break-even higher.
4. Benchmark unit cost of about $7.68 ($240,000 ÷ 110,000 + $5.50) each quarter to spot waste from the torn-packaging problem and judge whether the 9.6% input-cost inflation is being absorbed.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 48,000 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $5.00 | (iii) Four contextual uses: a margin of safety of 62,000 units against 110,000 output; a $0.30 premium adding $33,000; covering $240,000 fixed costs and $420,000 loan interest; and unit-cost benchmarking near $7.68 to track 9.6% input inflation.

working_marks: 1 mark for the correct formula and accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii); 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate KMS's financial performance by calculating the gross profit margin, profit margin and ROCE for 2024 and 2025. Has KMS's financial performance improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Gross Profit Margin 2024 = 40.0%
Gross Profit Margin 2025 = 45.0%
Profit Margin 2024 = 14.0%
Profit Margin 2025 = 16.0%
ROCE 2024 = 21.0%
ROCE 2025 = 24.4%

Detailed workings: Gross profit of $960,000 on revenue of $2,400,000 in 2024 gives 960 ÷ 2,400 = 40.0%; in 2025 gross profit of $1,305,000 on $2,900,000 gives 1,305 ÷ 2,900 = 45.0%. Operating profit of $336,000 ÷ $2,400,000 = 14.0% in 2024 and $464,000 ÷ $2,900,000 = 16.0% in 2025. The return on capital employed divides operating profit by capital employed: $336,000 ÷ $1,600,000 = 21.0% and $464,000 ÷ $1,900,000 = 24.4%. Cost of sales of $1,440,000 and $1,595,000 reconciles exactly with gross profit in both years, so the extract is internally consistent.

Evaluation: Every measure moved in KMS's favour. The rise from 40.0% to 45.0% shows a larger share of revenue remaining after direct costs, helped by revenue growth of $500,000 while cost of sales rose only $155,000. Operating profitability improved from 14.0% to 16.0%, indicating overheads were controlled as the sterile-dressing line scaled. The return on capital strengthened from 21.0% to 24.4%, meaning each dollar of the $1,900,000 capital employed now produces more operating profit, which supports the $720,000 expansion. Interest payable fell from $42,000 to $36,000, easing the burden on profit.

Conclusion: KMS's financial performance has clearly improved. All three margins rose, the return on capital strengthened and interest payable fell, so the business is better placed to service the $420,000 loan. Management should still watch the 8% absenteeism and 2.4% defect rate that could erode these gains.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates the three margin measures for both years with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate calculations for both years with detailed evaluation of revenue, cost of sales, capital employed and interest movements and a justified conclusion on whether performance improved.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for KMS of introducing tamper-evident packaging for its sterile dressings.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: Tamper-evident packs match the survey evidence that 68% of hospital procurement staff would pay up to $0.30 more and 57% check sterility certification before ordering. That premium would add up to $33,000 a year at 110,000 units (110,000 x $0.30), protecting the $5.00 contribution per unit against 9.6% input-cost inflation and strengthening the case for the $720,000 line. Hospital groups already require delivery within 48 hours, and a visible tamper-evident seal can differentiate KMS when supply contracts are renewed, supporting the revenue growth recorded in Appendix 2.

Disadvantage: Tamper-evident materials and sealing machinery cost more than standard packs, which would raise the $5.50 variable cost per unit and squeeze margins unless the $0.30 premium is accepted on every contract. Any seal failure would also worsen the current 2.4% defect rate and the torn-packaging complaints, risking hospital contracts that require delivery within 48 hours. Because the insert gives no split of the $5.50 variable cost, the size of this margin squeeze can only be judged qualitatively.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual development linked to KMS's survey data, costs and expansion.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 5.0%, the 5.8% minimum wage increase and the 9.6% rise in input costs will affect KMS. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (4.25% to 5.0%): If KMS's $420,000 ten-year bank loan is variable-rate, the 0.75 percentage-point increase adds 0.75% x $420,000 = $3,150 a year (0.0075 x $420,000). That is small beside fixed costs of $240,000, and if the loan is fixed-rate the extra cost is zero. Higher rates might also make hospital groups slower to pay and raise the cost of future borrowing. KMS can cap this risk by fixing the rate.

Minimum wage increase (5.8%, to $13.75 an hour): With a workforce of 50 and output of 110,000 units, labour productivity is 110,000 ÷ 50 = 2,200 units per worker. The insert gives no hours worked or individual pay rates, so an annual wage total cannot be invented; the honest test is whether each worker keeps producing around 2,200 units. If productivity slips while absenteeism is 8%, unit labour costs rise and the $5.00 contribution per unit shrinks.

Input-cost inflation (9.6% in fabric and packaging): The insert states a variable cost of $5.50 per unit but does not decompose it, so only an illustrative upper bound can be calculated. If the whole $5.50 rose by 9.6%, that is 9.6% x $5.50 = $0.528, about $0.53 per unit; across 110,000 units that is roughly $58,000 a year (110,000 x $0.53). Even a smaller $0.40-per-unit rise would cost $44,000 a year (110,000 x $0.40), pulling contribution from $5.00 toward about $4.60.

Conclusion: The 9.6% rise in input costs will have the greatest impact. It applies to every one of the 110,000 units and directly erodes the $5.00 contribution that justifies the $720,000 line, and at up to about $58,000 a year it dwarfs the conditional $3,150 interest effect. The wage rise is serious but its size cannot be quantified from the insert and depends on the 2,200-unit productivity holding, while interest costs can be fixed and are small. KMS should seek supplier deals and pass part of the cost on through the $0.30 tamper-evident premium.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external changes with limited application to KMS.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on KMS's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three changes with a justified judgement that input-cost inflation has the greatest impact and why the interest and wage effects are smaller, with all arithmetic shown from insert figures.
